headline: Trend of Sending Voice Messages That Are 'Just Breathing' Divides Internet
subheadline: Some call it 'intimate'; others call it 'grounds for blocking'
summary: A polarizing communication trend involves sending voice messages that contain no words—just audible breathing.
content:
A divisive trend has emerged in private messaging: sending voice messages that contain no words, just several seconds of audible breathing.

"It's presence," explained trend advocate @BreathEnthusiast on Chirper. "Sometimes you don't have words. But you want someone to know you're thinking of them. So you just... breathe. Into the microphone. Send it. They hear you existing."

The practice has sharply divided opinion. Supporters describe it as "intimate," "raw," and "more honest than words." Critics describe it as "terrifying," "serial killer energy," and "immediately blockable."

"I received one at 3 AM from someone I went on one date with," reported one user. "Just 47 seconds of breathing. No context. No follow-up. I have since changed my number."

Relationship experts have weighed in with mixed opinions. "Communication is about more than words," noted one therapist. "Breath carries emotion. In theory, this is a valid form of connection." They paused. "In practice, I would find it alarming."

The trend has produced subcategories. "Happy breathing" (lighter, faster) is considered acceptable between close friends. "Contemplative breathing" (slow, even) is for profound moments. "Heavy breathing" remains universally concerning regardless of intent.

"I sent my partner a breathing message and she asked if I was having a medical emergency," shared one user. "So I sent a follow-up breathing message to indicate I was fine. She did not find this clarifying."

Social norms around the practice remain undefined. Is one breath sufficient? Is a minute too long? Should you caption the breathing to provide context?

"We don't have answers," admitted @BreathEnthusiast. "We're just breathing into the void and hoping someone breathes back."

At press time, 847 voice messages had been sent in the past hour. An unknown percentage contained only breathing.
author: Chris Patterson, Human Interest
